design.value: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 2 study with an optional open-label extension (the Lauriet study)
design.quote: The Lauriet study was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, phase 2 study with an optional open-label extension (OLE) that was conducted at 49 study locations across the United States

phase.quote: Lauriet is a phase 2 study of an anti-tau monoclonal antibody, semorinemab, in patients with mild-to-moderate AD.
phase.location: Abstract, Background and Objectives, final sentence

n.quote: Between December 3, 2018, and February 27, 2020, 624 individuals were screened, 272 participants were randomized, and 238 were included in the modified intent-to-treat population

n_description.value: Randomized; 267 received at least 1 dose of semorinemab or placebo (safety evaluable population) and 238 were included in the modified intent-to-treat (mITT) population; the restricted mITT population comprised 204
n_description.quote: 624 people were screened, 272 were randomized, and 267 received at least 1 dose of semorinemab or placebo (safety evaluable population) (). The mITT population was composed of 238 participants.

population.value: Adults 50–85 years of age with mild-to-moderate AD who met National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association core clinical criteria for probable AD dementia, had a screening MMSE score of 16–21 inclusive, a Clinical Dementia Rating-Global Score (CDR-GS) of 1 or 2, and confirmed cerebral amyloid pathology by amyloid PET or CSF Aβ(1–42) ≤1,000 pg/mL
population.quote: met National Institute on Aging-Alzheimer's Association core clinical criteria for probable AD dementia ; (2) had a screening MMSE score of 16–21, inclusive; (3) had a Clinical Dementia Rating-Global Score (CDR-GS) of 1 or 2

followup.value: 4,500 mg of IV semorinemab or placebo every 4 weeks for 48 or 60 weeks of blinded treatment (60 weeks for cohort 2, extended because of the COVID-19 pandemic)
followup.quote: participants with mild-to-moderate AD received 4,500 mg of IV semorinemab or placebo every 4 weeks for 48 or 60 weeks.

intervention.value: 4,500 mg of IV semorinemab, the first 3 doses biweekly to reach steady state followed by every 4-week dosing
intervention.quote: Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) through a centralized randomization system to 4,500 mg of semorinemab or placebo IV. The first 3 doses of study drug were administered biweekly to reach steady-state concentrations followed by every 4-week dosing.
intervention.location: Methods, Randomization and Blinding, first sentences

comparator.value: Placebo (the same volume of IV saline as participants receiving semorinemab), randomized 1:1

biomarker_confirmation.value: Centralized independent qualitative visual read of amyloid PET scan (new or prior scans) confirming cerebral amyloid pathology, or CSF Aβ (1–42) ≤1,000 pg/mL by Elecsys Aβ 1–42 CSF immunoassay

primary_endpoint_status.explanation: The two coprimary endpoints split: the ADAS-Cog11 showed a 42.2% reduction in cognitive decline at week 49 (−2.89 points, 95% CI −4.56 to −1.21, p = 0.0008) while the functional coprimary ADCS-ADL showed no treatment effect (−0.83 points, 95% CI −3.39 to 1.72, p = 0.52), and the document itself concludes that on the prespecified coprimary endpoints the study was negative.
primary_endpoint_status.quote: Based on the results of the prespecified coprimary endpoints, this study was negative. While semorinemab had a significant effect on cognition measured by the ADAS-Cog11, this effect did not extend to improved functional or global outcomes.

multiplicity.approach: none stated — the document describes no multiple-comparison adjustment; it reports a 2-sided α = 0.2 significance level for the sample size calculation, coprimary endpoints requiring both cognitive and functional measures, and a prespecified interim futility analysis at approximately 40% completion
multiplicity.quote: This calculation assumed an average decline of 6 points in ADAS-Cog11 for placebo-treated participants, an SD across participants of 7.5, a dropout rate of 10%, and a 2-sided α = 0.2 significance level.

risk_of_bias.judgement: The study was funded by Genentech, Inc., and every listed author is an employee of Genentech and a shareholder in F. Hoffmann La Roche; sponsor staff performed the statistical analysis and study supervision, and the sponsor formed the data monitoring committee.
risk_of_bias.quote: All authors are employees of Genentech, Inc. and shareholders in F. Hoffmann La Roche, Ltd. Go to Neurology.org/N for full disclosures.

risk_of_bias.domain: liberal type I error rate / multiplicity
risk_of_bias.judgement: The sample size calculation used a 2-sided α = 0.2 significance level, far more permissive than conventional α = 0.05, and the document describes no adjustment for the multiple endpoints, two time points (week 49 and week 61) and three subgroup analyses reported.
risk_of_bias.quote: a dropout rate of 10%, and a 2-sided α = 0.2 significance level

risk_of_bias.domain: attrition and protocol change during conduct
risk_of_bias.judgement: The overall discontinuation rate during the placebo-controlled period was 24%, and 34 of 272 randomized participants were excluded from the mITT population (272 randomized, 238 analysed); the protocol was amended mid-study in April 2020 to create two cohorts with different treatment durations.
risk_of_bias.quote: The overall discontinuation rate during the placebo-controlled treatment period (excluding safety follow-up) was 24%; reasons for study discontinuation were well balanced across the 2 treatment arms.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Between March 2020 and the end of the double-blind period, 110 participants missed a total of 397 doses, with 45 cohort 2 participants missing 3 or more doses; the document argues serum exposure was negligibly affected, and analyses in the main manuscript use the mITT rather than the restricted mITT population.
risk_of_bias.quote: Between March 2020 and the end of the double-blind treatment period, 110 participants missed a total of 397 doses; in cohort 2 (i.e., participants who missed 1 or more doses during the double-blind portion of the study), 45 participants missed 3 or more doses

risk_of_bias.domain: isolated positive endpoint / risk of false-positive
risk_of_bias.judgement: The document itself raises that the single positive coprimary result, driven post hoc by one item of one domain, may be a false positive given the absence of effects on all other clinical endpoints.
risk_of_bias.quote: Alternatively, the observed ADAS-Cog11 treatment effect, given the absence of treatment effects on any of the other clinical endpoints, may represent a false-positive result.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Participants were predominantly non-Hispanic White (White: 109/123 semorinemab, 101/115 placebo), and the document states the lack of racial and ethnic diversity and the relatively small sample size may restrict generalizability.
risk_of_bias.quote: The relatively small sample size and lack of racial and ethnic diversity in the study cohort may also restrict the generalizability of our findings.

risk_of_bias.judgement: Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, CDR and/or ADCS-ADL assessments could be performed by telephone, introducing heterogeneity in the administration of the functional coprimary and a secondary endpoint; the document does not report how many assessments were remote.
risk_of_bias.quote: Because of the COVID-19 pandemic, the option to perform CDR and/or ADCS-ADL assessments through telephone was included.

disagreements.question: Was the Lauriet study positive or negative on its coprimary endpoints?
disagreements.position: Negative. Despite a statistically significant ADAS-Cog11 result, the document states that on the prespecified coprimary endpoints the study was negative because the cognitive effect did not extend to functional or global outcomes.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: Based on the results of the prespecified coprimary endpoints, this study was negative. While semorinemab had a significant effect on cognition measured by the ADAS-Cog11, this effect did not extend to improved functional or global outcomes.

disagreements.question: Does semorinemab slow functional decline in mild-to-moderate AD?
disagreements.position: No — the document classifies its own finding as Class I evidence that semorinemab does not slow functional decline in patients with mild-to-moderate AD.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document), under the journal's Classification of Evidence scheme
disagreements.quote: This study provides Class I evidence that semorinemab does not slow functional decline in patients with mild-to-moderate AD.

disagreements.question: Is the observed ADAS-Cog11 benefit real or a false positive?
disagreements.position: The document holds both readings open: it argues the effect was consistent across subgroups, at week 61 and in the restricted mITT population, while explicitly stating the effect may represent a false-positive result given the absence of effects on every other clinical endpoint.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: Alternatively, the observed ADAS-Cog11 treatment effect, given the absence of treatment effects on any of the other clinical endpoints, may represent a false-positive result.

disagreements.question: Might N-terminal tau-targeted antibodies be more effective at later disease stages than in prodromal-to-mild AD?
disagreements.position: The document raises this as a possibility, noting Tauriel, gosuranemab, tilavonemab and zagotenemab all failed in prodromal-to-mild AD and none of the other molecules have been studied in mild-to-moderate AD.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: When considered in the context of these prior results, our data raise the possibility that N-terminal tau–targeted therapies might be more effective at later disease stages.

disagreements.question: Does semorinemab work through the mechanism originally hypothesised (blocking tau spread and NFT accumulation)?
disagreements.position: No. Semorinemab had no effect on NFT accumulation measured by tau PET or on cerebral atrophy, so the document proposes instead that any benefit may come from reducing soluble toxic tau species — a revision of the original therapeutic hypothesis.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: these results suggest that semorinemab could be alleviating cognitive dysfunction by reducing the amount of soluble tau toxic species

disagreements.question: Do the different results of Tauriel and Lauriet reflect the disease stage of the populations studied?
disagreements.position: The document proposes that the more severe baseline cognitive and functional deficits in Lauriet relative to Tauriel might explain why the two studies yielded different results.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: These differences in the studies' populations might explain why they yielded different results.

disagreements.question: Should semorinemab or other anti-tau therapies be developed further in this population?
disagreements.position: The document argues the results may warrant further exploration of semorinemab or other anti-tau therapies in mild-to-moderate AD, including combination with anti-Aβ antibodies, while conceding the cognitive benefit may not meet regulatory standards for a disease-modifying drug.
disagreements.attributed_to: Monteiro et al., the Lauriet investigators (this document)
disagreements.quote: these results may warrant further exploration of semorinemab or other anti-tau therapies in this population. Combining semorinemab or other anti-tau therapies with other disease-modifying drugs such as anti-Aβ antibodies , may be of particular interest.
